content:
As real-time ray tracing and path tracing continue to push modern gaming hardware to its limits, researchers are exploring increasingly clever ways to reduce their computational overhead without relying exclusively on more powerful hardware.
Researchers at China's Wuhan University have developed a promising ray tracing optimization algorithm dubbed BMA (Bounding-Volume Mapping Heuristic Mapping Algorithm), which achieves up to 1.59x faster rendering while maintaining high image quality and introducing negligible memory overhead.
![A diagram illustrating ray tracing shows a camera, image plane, light source, and a scene object, with labeled arrows for 'View Ray' and 'Shadow Ray'.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/RTRT.jpg)
BMA Accelerates Ray Tracing By Intelligently Skipping Redundant BVH Traversal Operations
Modern ray tracing implementations rely on Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVHs), tree-like acceleration structures that allow rays to efficiently locate potentially intersecting geometry without individually testing every triangle within a scene.
However, repeatedly traversing these structures remains computationally expensive, particularly when simulating multiple light bounces in path-traced environments.
![A diagram titled 'BVH ALGORITHM' shows a hierarchical tree structure with a blue 3D model of a rabbit and bounding boxes.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/BVH-Algorithm-Rabbit-Diagram.jpg)
Detailed in a research paper published in Computers, BMA exploits the spatial coherence of rays originating from neighboring pixels. It samples representative rays across image tiles, estimates their likely traversal paths, and uses these predictions to let subsequent rays begin traversal deeper within the BVH.
Essentially, the algorithm allows rays to take computational shortcuts rather than repeatedly navigating the same branches of an acceleration structure.
The researchers evaluated BMA against an unmodified implementation of Intel's open-source Embree ray tracing library, rendering 100 frames at 1080p with a maximum path length of five.
The Sponza benchmark demonstrated particularly impressive results, with approximately 48% fewer BVH traversal operations and a 37% reduction in rendering time.
Meanwhile, additional memory consumption remained below 1% across all tested scenes.
![A multi-part diagram titled The final rendering result features a BVH traversal path sampling and convolution process applied to a 3D scene.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/BMA-scaled.jpg)
![A bar chart titled 'memory change ratio' shows the Cornell_box model has the highest memory change ratio near 0.6%, while other models like Buddha and Sponza are slightly lower.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Memory.jpg)
BMA Could Complement Existing Ray Tracing Optimizations, But There Are Some Caveats
Unlike conventional, mathematically exact traversal optimizations, BMA trades a small degree of rendering accuracy for improved performance. Nevertheless, all tested scenes achieved PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) values exceeding 35 dB and SSIM (Structural Similarity Index Measure) scores above 0.90.
![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/files/placeholder-mobile.png)
![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/files/placeholder-desktop.png)
![A bar chart titled 'PSNR' shows that the 'Cornell_box' image has the highest PSNR value compared to other images like 'Dragon' and 'Buddha'.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/PSNR.jpg)
Visual inaccuracies were primarily noticeable around thin geometry and object boundaries.
![A side-by-side comparison of two images of chairs labeled '(a) Reference image without BMA' and '(b) Rendered image with BMA applied.'](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Image-Quality-scaled.jpg)
The current BMA implementation focuses on CPU-side BVH traversal, with GPU and potentially NPU acceleration representing avenues for further development. The researchers also identify high-resolution rendering, including 8K gaming, as a potential application.
Interestingly, BMA could theoretically complement several recent ray tracing advancements we've covered, including AMD's RT-MLAS technology, NVIDIA's RTX Mega Geometry technology, and Microsoft's latest DirectX Raytracing enhancements. While these technologies primarily address the computational and memory overhead associated with constructing, updating, and managing acceleration structures for increasingly complex ray-traced geometry, BMA tackles a complementary bottleneck: the computational cost of traversing these structures.
Combining more efficient acceleration structures with intelligent traversal algorithms could help alleviate multiple ray tracing bottlenecks simultaneously.
While BMA's performance benefits in actual games remain unproven, the research provides another encouraging example of how algorithmic innovations could make computationally demanding path-traced visuals more accessible on future gaming hardware.
